extracted.intended_audience: communication scholars, political communication researchers, journalists, and graduate students
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical and practical criteria for identifying, describing, and evaluating 'frames' in communicated texts (especially news) — how frames are constructed, how they operate, where they reside, and how to study their effects on publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing as selection and salience (four framing functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing essentially involves selection and salience: to frame is to select some aspects of a perceived reality and make them more salient in a communicating text so as to promote a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and/or treatment recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames typically diagnose, evaluate, and prescribe. A single sentence can perform more than one of these four functions, and a frame in a particular text may not include all four. Example: the 'cold war' frame highlighted certain events as problems, identified causal agents, offered moral judgments, and recommended particular solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frames' locations in the communication process
rubrics_metrics.description: Frames exist in (at least) four locations: the communicator, the text, the receiver, and the culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicators are guided by frames/schemata in deciding what to say; texts contain frames manifested by presence/absence of key-words, stock phrases, stereotyped images, sources, and thematically reinforcing clusters of facts or judgments; receivers' frames may or may not reflect text/communicator intentions; culture is the stock of commonly invoked frames. Analysis should attend to all four locations rather than to text alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience as mechanism and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Salience means making a piece of information more noticeable, meaningful, or memorable to audiences; increasing salience raises the probability that receivers will perceive, process, and store the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Texts increase salience through placement, repetition, or association with culturally familiar symbols, but a single well-placed mention can be salient if it fits receiver schemata. Because salience is an interaction of text and receiver, the mere detection of a frame in a text by researchers does not guarantee influence on audience thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and omission (what frames omit matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frames define problems by selecting some aspects and omitting others; omissions are as critical as inclusions in guiding audience interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames simultaneously direct attention toward certain features and away from others; analysts should identify both what is emphasized and what is excluded. Examples: Kahneman & Tversky experiments and Edelman's discussion of how classification alters perceived character, causes, and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic audience effects and role of schemata
rubrics_metrics.description: Frames tend to have common effects on large portions of the receiving audience but not universally; framing effects depend on receivers' existing schemata, knowledge, and cognitive activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect framing to influence those with congruent or incomplete schemata more strongly; well-informed or cognitively active individuals may resist frame effects. Empirical claims about framing effects should consider variability across audience segments and conditions that mitigate influence (per Gamson, Zaller, Kahneman & Tversky, Iyengar).

rubrics_metrics.name: News frames as imprints of power and contested framing
rubrics_metrics.description: In political news, the frame in a news text is the imprint of power — reflecting the identity of actors or interests that competed to dominate the text — and frames can be self-reinforcing by defining the bounds of acceptable discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame analysis of news should examine which elites or actors shaped the frame, which alternatives were excluded as 'not newsworthy', and how that exclusion reduced the chances of alternative frames gaining traction (illustrated by pre-war Iraq coverage). Assess how frames become institutionalized (e.g., terms like 'affirmative action').

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of 'dominant meaning' for audience autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant meaning consists of the problem, causal, evaluative, and treatment interpretations with the highest probability of being noticed, processed, and accepted by the most people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To argue that messages are polysemic or that audiences reframe texts, researchers must demonstrate real-world reframing (not artifacts of research conditions such as leading focus groups or suggestive interviews). Identifying dominant meaning requires showing congruence between text frames and common audience schemata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications for journalistic objectivity (assessing balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists may follow norms of 'objectivity' yet still convey a dominant framing that prevents balanced audience assessments; objectivity in form does not guarantee balance in framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists aiming for genuinely balanced reporting should make alternative interpretations equally salient rather than merely including scattered oppositional facts. This requires a more active, sophisticated role for reporters than formulaic objectivity affords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content analysis informed by framing: measure salience and clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Content analysis should identify and describe frames, measuring the salience of elements and the relationships among the most salient clusters, rather than simply tallying positive/negative terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coders must be guided by a framing paradigm to avoid misrepresenting the media messages audiences actually pick up. Measure placement, repetition, association, and thematic reinforcement to capture what is truly salient for audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing's consequences for public opinion measurement and democratic theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Because elites can control issue framing, frames can determine measured 'public opinion'; differing frames can produce different majority preferences, complicating inferences about what the public 'really' wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey and voting results under different frames do not straightforwardly identify the 'correct' public preference. Analysts and democratic theorists should account for framing when interpreting polls, voting behavior, and claims about majority will; resolving which frame is most accurate or fair often requires normative agreement among elites and citizens.
